extracted.intended_audience: registered USPTO patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), OED counsel, and participants in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, procedures, and factors used to evaluate practitioner misconduct and to determine sanctions in USPTO disciplinary proceedings under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. part 11. Includes service/default rules, substantive conduct rules (competence, communication, safekeeping), burden of proof, and sanctioning factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence — 37 C.F.R. § 11.101
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must provide competent representation to a client, which requires exercising 'the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to produce work that competently and accurately characterizes an invention or otherwise perform required legal/scientific tasks can constitute a violation (illustrated by the Shah matter where drafts were unsatisfactory and delayed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence/Promptness — 37 C.F.R. § 11.103
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must 'act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not timely submitting required filings (e.g., failing to respond to an Office action resulting in abandonment despite being retained and paid to do so) violates § 11.103 (illustrated by the Dunnington matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Client Communications — 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3), (a)(4), and (b)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the client's matters; promptly comply with reasonable requests for information; and explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of misconduct: failing to inform a client that an application was abandoned; making false statements about filings; failing to respond to repeated client inquiries. The rule requires reasonable status updates, timely responses to information requests, and sufficient explanation for client decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safekeeping Client Property / Return of Unearned Fees — 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must duly safeguard any property of clients or third persons in the practitioner's possession, including by 'promptly deliver[ing] to the client or third person any funds or other property that the client or third person is entitled to receive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting advance fees and failing to refund unearned fees (or failing to remit government fees earmarked for filing) may violate § 11.115(d). The decision treats retaining unearned client funds after not performing work as a violation when shown by the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct After Termination — 37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon termination of representation, a practitioner must 'take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect a client's interests, such as … surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled and refunding any advance payment of fee or expense that has not been earned or incurred.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to return unearned advance fees or ceasing communication after termination violates this provision (illustrated by the Shah matter where the client terminated and did not receive a refund).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Cooperate in Disciplinary Investigation — 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner has a duty to cooperate with an OED disciplinary investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not responding to RFIs, Lack of Response notifications, or other investigative correspondence is a violation. The decision explains that failure to cooperate undermines the disciplinary system and is an aggravating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty / Fraud / Deceit / Misrepresentation — 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules proscribe 'conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.' Dishonest conduct is characterized by a lack of truth, honesty, straightforwardness, or trustworthiness; 'deceit' and 'misrepresentation' are defined in ordinary/legal dictionaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making false statements to a client about filings (e.g., asserting materials were submitted when they were not) constitutes a § 11.804(c) violation. The decision cites dictionary and case-law definitions to identify dishonest conduct and deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct Prejudicial to the Administration of Justice — 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to cooperate in disciplinary investigations is prejudicial because it undermines public trust and the integrity of attorney self-regulation; thus noncooperation can violate § 11.804(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to Timely Answer / Default Judgment Consequences — 37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent fails to file an Answer by regulatory deadlines (including after service by publication), the respondent is deemed to have admitted the allegations, and default judgment (including exclusion) may follow. Examples of precedent decisions granting default judgment are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of Process and Correspondence Address Requirements — 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.11 and 11.35
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered USPTO practitioner must notify the OED Director of the postal address for the practitioner's office and provide written notice of any address change within 30 days (§ 11.11). Service of a Complaint may be completed by mailing a copy to the correspondence address provided (§ 11.35(a)(2)); if unclear whether served, publication in the Official Gazette may effectuate service (§ 11.35(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision details attempts: certified mail, first-class mail, process server, email notifications, and service by publication when other methods failed. Practitioners are required to keep correspondence address current to ensure service is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and Standard of Proof — 37 C.F.R. § 11.49
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with default, the decision references that the regulatory burden is clear and convincing; however, failure to answer operates as an admission of the Complaint's factual allegations for purposes of default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning Factors to Consider — 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining appropriate sanctions, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies these four factors to justify exclusion, explaining how each factor weighed (e.g., fiduciary duty breach, knowing/willful conduct, actual client harm, and aggravating factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and Mitigating Factors (ABA STANDARDS § 9.1, § 9.22 examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The STANDARDS list aggravating and mitigating factors to guide sanctions (e.g., prior disciplinary offenses; dishonest or selfish motive; bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding; substantial experience in the practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court used these factors: prior warning/public reproval (aggravating), possible dishonest motive (considered but not fully established), bad faith obstruction (failure to cooperate/respond), and substantial experience (aggravating because experienced practitioners should know rules). These factors can increase or decrease sanction severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental State / Willfulness in Discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental state (intentional, knowing, or negligent) is decisive for culpability; 'willfulness' generally refers to conduct that goes beyond negligence and means the wrongdoer either knew or showed reckless disregard for whether conduct was prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional or knowing conduct is sanctioned more severely than negligent conduct. The decision treats the respondent's admitted willful conduct as evidence of knowing/reckless disregard, warranting a severe sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of Discipline — Protection and Administration of Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of practitioner discipline is to protect the public and the administration of justice, not merely to punish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions should focus on protecting the public and preserving the integrity of the legal profession and disciplinary system; exclusion is appropriate when a practitioner is unlikely to properly discharge professional duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion / Reinstatement Rules — 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner excluded from practice before USPTO is subject to responsibilities during suspension/exclusion (see § 11.58) and is eligible to apply for reinstatement no earlier than five years from the effective date of the exclusion (§ 11.60(b)), subject to compliance with regulatory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision orders exclusion and notifies respondent of obligations under § 11.58 and appeal rights under § 11.55. Reinstatement eligibility requires full compliance with the listed requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Precedent and Regulatory Remedies in Disciplinary Decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO decisions routinely cite prior disciplinary cases and the ABA STANDARDS as guidance for findings and sanctions (e.g., In re Whitney; In re Morishita; In re Schwedler; STANDARDS §§ 1.1, 3.0, 9.1, 9.22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions compare facts to prior cases and invoke established standards to justify findings and sanctions; practitioners should be aware that precedent and STANDARDS inform the application of rules and selection of sanctions.
